mcqs.question: Why is RIP's hop-count metric a poor fit for a network with mixed link speeds, like a mix of fiber and slow satellite hops?
options: Hop count treats every hop as equally costly regardless of actual bandwidth or latency, so it can choose a path over several slow links over a shorter path with fewer, faster ones
RIP cannot function at all on networks with more than one link type
RIP requires all links in the network to have identical bandwidth by protocol specification
Hop count only works correctly on wireless links, not wired ones
mcqs.explanation: The core limitation is that hop count is blind to link quality — a slow satellite hop counts identically to a fast fiber hop, so RIP can pick a technically 'shorter' but actually slower path. RIP does function on mixed-speed networks, just suboptimally (the cannot-function-at-all claim is false); there's no such uniform-bandwidth requirement in the protocol (the uniform-bandwidth-requirement claim is false); and hop count isn't wireless-specific (the wireless-only claim is false).

mcqs.question: How does split horizon prevent the count-to-infinity problem?
options: By encrypting routing updates so stale routes can't be forged
By preventing a router from advertising a route back to the same neighbor it originally learned that route from, breaking the loop where two routers keep re-confirming stale information to each other
By requiring every router to wait exactly 30 seconds before accepting any route update
By replacing hop count with a bandwidth-based metric
mcqs.explanation: Split horizon's specific fix is withholding a route advertisement from the exact neighbor it came from, which directly breaks the cyclic re-confirmation that causes count-to-infinity. It has nothing to do with encryption (the encryption claim), doesn't rely on a fixed wait timer (the fixed-wait-timer claim), and doesn't change the metric type at all (the metric-replacement claim).

mcqs.question: Why can packets be dropped or looped specifically during the period before a network has converged?
options: Because routers deliberately drop all traffic during convergence for safety
Because convergence only affects link-state protocols, not distance-vector ones
Because different routers may temporarily hold inconsistent views of the topology, so one router's forwarding decision may conflict with another's until they all agree on the same updated state
Because packets are physically incompatible with routers that haven't finished converging
mcqs.explanation: The risk exists precisely because routers don't all update atomically — during the window where some have the new topology and others still have stale information, forwarding decisions can conflict, causing drops or loops. Routers don't deliberately halt traffic (the deliberate-drop claim), convergence applies to both protocol families, not just link-state (the link-state-only claim), and there's no physical incompatibility concept here (the physical-incompatibility claim).
